messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to have 2 sliders controlling each other? The code below represents an endless loop if there are both updateSlidersInput() present. If either one of updateSlidersInput() is deleted that would be a typical slider "a" controls slider "b" solution. I tried eventReactive() with no success.

library(shiny)
ui <- fluidPage(
      titlePanel("Test"),
       sidebarLayout(
       sidebarPanel(
       sliderInput("Slider1", "Slider1", min = 1, max = 10, value = 5),
       sliderInput("Slider2", "Slider2", min = 1, max = 10, value = 1),
    ),
    mainPanel(  )
  )
)
server <- shinyServer(function(input, output, session) {
          v <- reactiveValues(x=NULL)

          observeEvent(input$Slider1, {v$x <- input$Slider1
                                       updateSliderInput(session, "Slider2", value=v$x )
                                       print(paste0(v$x, " slider1"))
          })
          observeEvent(input$Slider2, {v$x <- input$Slider2
                                       updateSliderInput(session, "Slider1", value=v$x )
                                       print(paste0(v$x, " slider2"))
          })
})
shinyApp(ui, server)

messages.subject: Re: two sliders controlling each other
messages.subject_clean: two sliders controlling each other
messages.body_plain:
You could do something like this:

library(shiny)
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Test"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("Slider1", "Slider1", min = 1, max = 10, value = 5),
      sliderInput("Slider2", "Slider2", min = 1, max = 10, value = 1)

    ),
    mainPanel(  )
  )
)
server <- shinyServer(function(input, output, session) {
  v <- reactiveValues(x = NULL)

  observeEvent(input$Slider1, {
    v$x <- input$Slider1

  })
  observeEvent(input$Slider2, {
    v$x <- input$Slider2

  })

  observeEvent(v$x, {
    if (v$x != input$Slider1) {
      updateSliderInput(session, "Slider1", value = v$x)
    }

    if (v$x != input$Slider2) {
      updateSliderInput(session, "Slider2", value = v$x)
    }
  })
})

shinyApp(ui, server)

Note that, by default, the order of the observeEvents isn't guaranteed, so v$x could hypothetically update from Slider1 before Slider2 or vice versa. If you want to set the order, you can add `priority = 10` to one of the observeEvents. For example, if you add it to the second one, then the sliders will be set to 5, the starting value for Slider1.

-Winston

messages.subject: R svgPanZoom and "locator"
messages.subject_clean: R svgPanZoom and "locator"
messages.body_plain:
Dear shiny developers,

I try to develop an shiny app for analysis of biological images, i.e. the shiny app will upload an image (of a biological tissue for instance) and the user will have to click on the image to place the nucleus of each cell to finally get the coordinates of each nucleus (and thus draw a map of the tissue).

Sometimes the cells are so small that users will have to zoom on the picture to see correctly the nucleus.

So I tried to develop an app allowing users to zoom on their picture. Basically I planned to use the zoom of the shiny plotOutput (http://shiny.rstudio.com/gallery/plot-interaction-zoom.html) but few weeks ago I found this beautiful package of svgPanZoom and I would like to combine it with my shiny app.

For including svgPanZoom in the app no problem, but it gets more complicated when I try to have a "locator" in the app (like a "clickId" from the function plotOutput). I can't get the solution of my problem...
I would have probably to custom the renderSvgPanZoom function but I did not reach my goal.

Do you have an idea ?

Here I put a simple code for renderSvgPanZoom. Here I would like to include a clickId or a locator in this script:

library(shiny)
library(svglite)
library(svgPanZoom)
library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)

data.df <- data.frame(Plant = c("Plant1", "Plant1", "Plant1", "Plant2", "Plant2",
                                "Plant2"), Type = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3), Axis1 = c(0.2, -0.4, 0.8, -0.2, -0.7,
                                                                                 0.1), Axis2 = c(0.5, 0.3, -0.1, -0.3, -0.1, -0.8))

ui <- shinyUI(bootstrapPage(

  svgPanZoomOutput(outputId = "main_plot")

))

server = shinyServer(function(input, output) {
  output$main_plot <- renderSvgPanZoom({
    p <- ggplot(data.df, aes(x = Axis1, y = Axis2, shape = Plant, color = Type)) + geom_point(size = 5)
    svgPanZoom(p, controlIconsEnabled = T)
  })
})

runApp(list(ui=ui,server=server))

I try to find an answer on internet but I found nothing even by asking questions (perhaps I was not clear enough, I hope this message will be clear enough) http://stackoverflow.com/questions/39817784/r-svgpanzoom-customize-size-and-add-locator?noredirect=1#comment66926839_39817784, https://github.com/timelyportfolio/svgPanZoom/issues/16

Thank you very much in advance for any help !

Have a nice day.

Charlotte

messages.subject_clean: Problem restoring DT filter from bookmark URL in shiny app
messages.body_plain:
I'm having problems restoring the state of a DT data table from a url-encoded bookmark in a Shiny app.
I created an onRestored() handler to update the table using a DT proxy.  The problem comes from the data table's global filter (search) box.  If there is text in the box, restoring works fine - both the filter value and any row selections are restored.  However, if the search is empty I get this error:
Error in RestoreContext initialization: Failed to parse URL parameter "resTable_search"
The app displays correctly but any row selections are not restored.

I edited the bookmark URL to remove the resTable_search parameter; in that case the table row selections restore.  However, I haven't figured out how to code something that will eliminate this input only when it's blank.

I would appreciate advice on how to trap/handle the case of an empty value.

Thanks!

The attached file 'app.R' reproduces the error in a minimal example.  Here is the onRestored function from that app; resTable is the DT table I want to restore.
  # restore table selection and search
  onRestored(function(state) {
    message("Input:",print(state$input))
    DT::selectRows(resTable_proxy,
                   state$input$resTable_rows_selected)

    # updating DataTable global filter
    # works if the search box has text but not if it's empty.
    # also, selected rows aren't restored.
    # tried prefixing with req(state$input$resTable_search) - still get error
    # tried wrapping in if(isTruthy(state$input$resTable_search)) - still get error
    req(state$input$resTable_search)
    DT::updateSearch(resTable_proxy,
                     keywords = list(global = state$input$resTable_search,
                                     columns = NULL))
  })

messages.body_plain:
I have a system mostly running that proxies requests to Shiny Server. The reason for this proxy is so that I can run custom authentication (for delivering media through IMS LTI). My proxy lives at https://my-host.com:8080/provider/ and it forwards to Shiny at http://localhost:3838/test/.

I need to pass information about the user from the authentication step on to Shiny, so I'm trying to edit the request to shiny to include URL parameters that identify the user. However, Shiny seems to ignore the edited request and use the request URI from the original request to the proxy:

A request to https://my-host.com:8080/provider/?key=value will result in the desired behavior, and session$clientData$url_search shows the query parameter key=value.
A request to https://my-host.com:8080/provider/ in which the proxy changes the URL and opens a new request Shiny shows the session$clientData from the original request, rather than the request that actually goes to Shiny.

Here's an access log excerpt for the second case. Note that the first request shows the correct query parameters as they are added by my proxy.

messages.subject: Debugging reactivity
messages.subject_clean: Debugging reactivity
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We are having a big issue debugging reactivity.  There is "sufficient" documentation about the reactivity logs when running Shiny through multiple-files (ui.R and server.R) in an Rstudio session.  However, we are trying to debug this using a single app.R file and through Shiny Server (Pro), not Rstudio.

How can we do this properly?

Also, I tried setting the SHINY_LOG_LEVEL environment variable, but I don't see any difference in logs.

The reason this is important to us right now is that while the app is starting up, there is roughly 10-12 seconds where "nothing" is happening, and we are trying to figure out what it is.  We have added withProgress to any reactive items we can find, but still can't pinpoint what is causing the huge delay.

Or better yet - is there a way to simply provide a "Loading ..." overlay until the app is actually ready to go?  Our users continue to click all over the place while the UI is still being put together, and it's really causing issues.

Any help is greatly appreciated.  Thank you!
~Laz Peterson

messages.subject_clean: Debugging reactivity
messages.body_plain:
There are a bunch of options to consider.

First off, I'd argue that having a checkboxGroupInput that large isn't a good user experience anyway. Have you considered using a selectize box? messages.body_plain:
Joe,

Your head is definitely in the right place ... We *DO NOT* need that many options in the checkboxGroupInput.  I have re-created the MySQL views so that we are sorting by "instance counts", and now the list of 2800+ is down to 764.  That number is something we can work with.  The amount of time it takes to process is now very minimal.

And yes, you are very right ... The user experience really isn't very fun when you have a list of nearly 3000 options in a checkbox group input.  So that's something I'll take care of ... (Specifically, we don't need any options where there are 0 pieces of data associated!)

Now, there are a couple other chunks of 3-4 seconds of time that is lost while loading the app. We would really like to troubleshoot this.

I added a withProgress to each of the renderUI objects in the app, but the first chunk of time lost still does not give any clue as to which process is taking up all that CPU time.

Any recommendation on the best way to approach that?

Aside from troubleshooting the performance for each little bit of the entire code, another option would be to simply block user input and display an overlay message with "Loading ..." (and maybe a cute animated image) until the entire app is loaded. What are your thoughts on that one?

Our biggest issue with our clients is that they continually say, "Oh, this isn't usable," or, "It crashes every time we use it."  But the fact is that they simply don't wait until things are ready.  I would really like to make sure they are unable to mess up the session, because that seems to be the first thing they do.

With all that being said, it would also be very nice to have some sort of progress indicator that encompasses everything (all reactive and non-reactive functions that are going on) so that the user can at least feel like they know something is going on, and the progress there.

How do Shiny users normally provide this type of function?

Ps, we love Shiny.  Our users though, they are not so wonderful.  Ha ha ha ... It seems they try their hardest to make our lives difficult!

Thanks again Joe.
~Laz

messages.subject: Re: Debugging reactivity
messages.subject_clean: Debugging reactivity
messages.body_plain:
First off, it's far easier to troubleshoot performance issues by reproducing them outside of Shiny Server, i.e. from within RStudio. If you simply can't do it anywhere but on Shiny Server, then you still have some options.

1) Use reactlog. This works for relatively small apps with not too many reactive expressions and outputs (the UI for the reactlog visualization tool doesn't scale well), and only in situations where the time is being lost in reactive expressions and outputs. You can enable this by putting the line "options(shiny.reactlog=TRUE)" at the top of app.R, then when viewing the app in the browser, hit Ctrl+F3 (or Cmd+F3 if you're on a Mac). If you're using Shiny v0.14, after you step through the "Running" (green) portion of a reactive expression or output, you'll see an elapsed time. Note that if an output A calls a reactive expression B, and A shows 310 milliseconds while B shows 290 milliseconds, it may be the case that A's time includes B's time (so A itself only spent 20 milliseconds on its non-B-related operations).

2) Collect a profile trace on the server, and load it into profvis. Call Rprof("path-to-somewhere-writable.Rprof", memory.profiling=TRUE) at the top of app.R, and then at some later point after everything has loaded (use an actionButton/observeEvent if you need to), call Rprof(NULL). Then download the .Rprof file to your local machine that's running RStudio, and use the profvis package to visualize it:
profvis::profvis(prof_input = "file.Rprof")

Or you can send me the file.Rprof and I'll see if I can make sense of it myself using profvis.

messages.subject: Re: Shiny Server Package Location

messages.body_plain:
Yeah, keep in mind that (by default) Shiny Server runs as the "shiny" user. So if you're doing library stuff on your normal user account, that will likely not affect what Shiny Server apps see. From an ssh prompt, you can use "sudo su - shiny" to change to the "shiny" user, then run R from that prompt, then call .libPaths() or system.file or remove.packages or whatever.

On Tue, Oct 11, 2016 at 1:11 PM Dean Attali <daat...@gmail.com> wrote:

> It's possible you installed the package another user and shiny has access to that user's library perhaps?
>
> If Shiny is able to use a package and you have no idea where that package is, what you can do is make shiny tell you where the package is. Just make a textOutput(), and in the renderText() function make it output `system.file(package = packagename)` and then in your app it'll show you the path
>
> On Tuesday, 11 October 2016 09:08:21 UTC-7, Josh wrote:

> First off, it's far easier to troubleshoot performance issues by reproducing them outside of Shiny Server, i.e. from within RStudio. If you simply can't do it anywhere but on Shiny Server, then you still have some options.
>
> 1) Use reactlog. This works for relatively small apps with not too many reactive expressions and outputs (the UI for the reactlog visualization tool doesn't scale well), and only in situations where the time is being lost in reactive expressions and outputs. You can enable this by putting the line "options(shiny.reactlog=TRUE)" at the top of app.R, then when viewing the app in the browser, hit Ctrl+F3 (or Cmd+F3 if you're on a Mac). If you're using Shiny v0.14, after you step through the "Running" (green) portion of a reactive expression or output, you'll see an elapsed time. Note that if an output A calls a reactive expression B, and A shows 310 milliseconds while B shows 290 milliseconds, it may be the case that A's time includes B's time (so A itself only spent 20 milliseconds on its non-B-related operations).
>
> 2) Collect a profile trace on the server, and load it into profvis. Call Rprof("path-to-somewhere-writable.Rprof", memory.profiling=TRUE) at the top of app.R, and then at some later point after everything has loaded (use an actionButton/observeEvent if you need to), call Rprof(NULL). Then download the .Rprof file to your local machine that's running RStudio, and use the profvis package to visualize it:

messages.subject_clean: Connection lost on spotty wifi
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a few shiny apps hosted on AWS that are intermittently crashing with a grey screen on a colleague's computer. Unfortunately I can't reproduce the crashes and it doesn't seem to be bug-related. My colleague has complained that the wifi in his office is very spotty so I suspect that he's losing connection to the server which closes the app. The crashing happens erratically, some times 5 seconds after he loses internet, sometimes after 1 minute or so. Is there any way to keep the connection to shiny server alive when the internet is bad? The keepalive timeout on nginx is not set (so i assume it's the default 75 seconds) and the crashes happen faster when an action is taken (e.g. something selected from a drop-down), so I assume that it's brought on by a failed http request.

So, in summary, can a shiny app be kept alive without an internet connection? Or are there any workarounds to mitigate internet connectivity issues?

Thanks

messages.body_plain:
I'm in Shiny, RStudio. I'm making an app that processes a user input in several steps, each step taking input from the previous step. At each step the user can set several parameters to process the input.

The workflow looks like this:

Step1: upload input from user

    obj_step1 <- eventReactive(input$actionButton1, {#function to upload input from user})
    output$step1 <- renderPlot({#function to display obj_step1})

Step2:

    obj_step2 <- eventReactive(input$actionbutton2, {#function to process obj_step1, taking several user given parameters from the ui with input$})
    output$step2 <- renderPlot({#function to display obj_step3})

Step3:

    obj_step3 <- eventReactive(input$actionbutton3, {#function to process obj_step2, taking several user given parameters from the ui with input$})
    output$step3 <- renderPlot({#function to display obj_step3})

Step4:

    obj_step4 <- eventReactive(input$actionbutton4, {#function to process obj_step3, taking several user given parameters from the ui with input$})
    output$step4 <- renderPlot({#function to display obj_step4})

messages.subject: Putting a plot from Shiny into an Excel using the "xlsx" package and then downloading it
messages.subject_clean: Putting a plot from Shiny into an Excel using the "xlsx" package and then downloading it
messages.body_plain:
Hello fellow shiny users.

I am running across a problem I can't seem to find any solution to on the various forums and websites.
I will share a relatively simple reproducible example that illustrates my problem.

I want to do the following: Upload some data, do some processing and analysis, then put the whole bunch of outputs into an Excel file and finally download it.
I have no trouble creating that Excel in the shiny server part, and putting dataframes/tables into it. But I can't put images in the Excel file.

It is because the AddPicture function from the xlsx package I use requires the following things:

____________________________________________________________________________
addPicture(file, sheet, scale=1, startRow=1, startColumn=1)

file
the absolute path to the image file.

sheet
a worksheet object as returned by createSheet or by subsetting getSheets. The picture will be added on this sheet at position startRow, startColumn.

"The absolute path to the image file" is the problem. I can't have an absolute path to the file, as when I execute a similar script with R. Or can I?
____________________________________________________________________________________________

Here is some code that shows the error:

If you execute it as it stands, you will be able to download an Excel file with a dataframe in the first sheet no problem. (Because there is no absolute path needed, just a dataframe object)
The part with #  in the server part is what bring me problems. You can uncomment it to see the error (Error : no applicable method for 'grid.draw' applied to an object of class "NULL" ) . Does anyone have an idea on how to solve this?

SERVER

library(shiny)
library(xlsx)
library(ggplot2)

server <- function(input, output) {

output$download.Excel <- downloadHandler(

  filename = function() { paste("Excelfile.xlsx")},
  content = function(file){
    example_plot=plot(1:10,1:10)
    Results_Workbook <- createWorkbook(type='xlsx')
    A=as.data.frame(matrix(2,2,2))
    sheet.1 <- createSheet(Results_Workbook, sheetName = "Data frame")
    addDataFrame(A, sheet=sheet.1, startRow=4, startColumn=2,row.names=FALSE)
    setColumnWidth(sheet.1,colIndex=c(1:100),colWidth=30)
    sheet.2 <- createSheet(Results_Workbook, sheetName = "Plot")
    # ggsave("plot",example_plot, device="emf")
    # addImage(file = "plot.emf", sheet = sheet.2, scale = 55,
    #          startRow = 4, startColumn = 4)
    saveWorkbook(Results_Workbook,file)
  }

)
}

UI

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Simple classification script with R/Shiny"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      downloadButton('download.Excel', 'Download')

    ),
    mainPanel(p("Description of the results")
    )
  )
)

Best regards,

Joël

messages.subject: Re: Data not available outside of observeEvent() statement?
messages.subject_clean: Data not available outside of observeEvent() statement?
messages.body_plain:
Like functions, observers create their own variable scope. By default, variable writes are local to each function/observer.

If you want to make x available to both the observer and the renderPrint, you'd need to declare "x <- NULL" outside of the observer (but still inside the shiny server function) and then assign to it from inside the observer with the <<- operator, e.g. "x <<- 1".

But simple variables do not trigger reactivity--assigning to x will not, by default, cause renderPrint to re-run. You need to specifically tell Shiny to treat x as a reactive variable, by calling makeReactiveBinding.

I haven't tried this but it should work:

server <- function (input,output) {
  x <- NULL
  makeReactiveBinding("x")

  observeEvent(input$button,{
    x <<- 1
  })

  observe({
    output$data <- renderPrint(x)
  })
}

Further reading:
http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Functions.html#lexical-scoping
http://shiny.rstudio.com/articles/scoping.html

messages.body_plain:
Sorry I never replied to this. You can use the object-oriented progress API (see ?shiny::Progress). You should be able to start the progress as the session starts, and close it at some later time (I'm assuming there's some easy place in your code that you definitely know everything's done processing--if not, we can talk about how to introduce that).

Here's an example:

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      uiOutput("ui1"),
      uiOutput("ui2")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      verbatimTextOutput("result")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  progress <- Progress$new(session)
  progress$set(message = "Please wait...")

  output$ui1 <- renderUI({
    Sys.sleep(3)
    numericInput("x", "x", 5)
  })

  output$ui2 <- renderUI({
    req(input$x)
    Sys.sleep(3)
    numericInput("y", "y", input$x * 2)
  })

  output$result <- renderPrint({
    req(input$x, input$y)

    if (!is.null(progress)) {
      progress$close()
      progress <<- NULL
    }

    input$x * input$y
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

This works for relatively small apps with not too many reactive expressions and outputs (the UI for the reactlog visualization tool doesn't scale well), and only in situations where the time is being lost in reactive expressions and outputs. You can enable this by putting the line "options(shiny.reactlog=TRUE)" at the top of app.R, then when viewing the app in the browser, hit Ctrl+F3 (or Cmd+F3 if you're on a Mac). If you're using Shiny v0.14, after you step through the "Running" (green) portion of a reactive expression or output, you'll see an elapsed time. Note that if an output A calls a reactive expression B, and A shows 310 milliseconds while B shows 290 milliseconds, it may be the case that A's time includes B's time (so A itself only spent 20 milliseconds on its non-B-related operations).
> >

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to retrieve information (in this case .html pages) from a persistent data storage ( in this case DropBox) implementing various posts and question found within the WWW such as http://shiny.rstudio.com/articles/persistent-data-storage.html.

Nonetheless, after many hours of trial and error I have not been able to make it work.

Below I am including a testing app.

The goal of the app is to retrieve html pages from DropBox by reactive names, move them to the app www folder and finally display the html pages in the app main panel.

I want to retrieve the documents from DropBox for two main reasons:

To save time when changing or adding html pages or any new information.

shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> upload all the bondle everytime it is updated.

Shinyapps.io accepts apps of upto 5G.

Your help is much appreciated.

Thanks in advance for your time.

Notes:

The rdrop2 code within the application were tested outside shiny and it worked.

The token and the .httr-oauth are within the Shiny App repository

This app works if the .html pages are within the app www folder

I am including as attachment the testing pages I am using to test the procedure.

The code below is one of many I have tried but I belief is the one that best resemble the one close to work.

#### Start of Shiny app ####

library(shiny)

library(rdrop2)

ui <- # Define UI for dataset viewer application

shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(

headerPanel("Test DropBox html Docs to Shiny"),

sidebarPanel(

selectInput("Cat", "Choose a Category:",

choices = c("A", "B")),

selectInput("Year", "Choose a Year:",

choices = c("2012", "2011")), width = 2),

mainPanel(

tabsetPanel(type = "tabs",

tabPanel("Html Pages", htmlOutput("viewReport"))), width = 10)

))

# The two lines below needs to be run just one time unless the token is deleted

# Create Token

# tokenF <- drop_auth()

# Save token

# saveRDS(tokenF, "droptoken.rds")

token <- readRDS("droptoken.rds")

server <- shinyServer(function(input, output) {

filePutReport <- reactive(

paste(input$Cat, "_", input$Year, "_Doc.html", sep = "")

)

reactive({

drop_get(paste("/Shiny_DB_Test/", filePutReport(), sep = ""),

dtoken = token)

# I have not bee able to drop_get directly to the www folder

file.copy(from = paste("./Shiny_Local/", filePutReport(), sep = ""),

to = "./Shiny_Local/www")

file.remove(paste("./Shiny_Local/", filePutReport(), sep = ""))

})

# Show Html Pages

output$viewReport <- renderUI({

tags$iframe(seamless = "seamless", width = "1400", height = "1000",

src = filePutReport())

})

})

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

Hello everybody !

I am still trying to zoom in an plot containing an image (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/shiny-discuss/svgPanZoom%7Csort:relevance/shiny-discuss/F3Y2yBO-mEY/JnbXJfywAAAJ).

A brief context for my app: the aim of this app would be to determine the structure of a biological tissue. So this app would upload an image of the tissue (a picture from a microscope for instance) and the user will have to click on the image to place the nucleus of each cell to finally get the coordinates of each nucleus (and thus draw a map of the tissue).

However, the problem is that sometimes the cells are so small that users will have to zoom on the picture to see correctly the nucleus.

1/ So I tried first to include this image in a plot. But when users zoom, the plot is correctly zoomed but not the image on the background. It remains with the same dimensions:

library(ggplot2)
library(Cairo)   # For nicer ggplot2 output when deployed on Linux

ui <- fluidPage(
  fluidRow(
    column(width = 4, class = "well",
           h4("Brush and double-click to zoom"),
           plotOutput("plot1", height = 300,
                      dblclick = "plot1_dblclick",
                      brush = brushOpts(
                        id = "plot1_brush",
                        resetOnNew = TRUE
                      )
           )
    )

  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Single zoomable plot (on left)
  ranges <- reactiveValues(x = NULL, y = NULL)

  # Write to a temporary PNG file
  outfile <- tempfile(fileext = ".jpg")

  jpeg(outfile)
  plot(rnorm(200), rnorm(200))
  dev.off()

  image <- readJPEG(outfile)

  g <- rasterGrob(image, interpolate=TRUE)

  output$plot1 <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
      geom_point() +
      coord_cartesian(xlim = ranges$x, ylim = ranges$y) +
      annotation_custom(g)
  })

  # When a double-click happens, check if there's a brush on the plot.
  # If so, zoom to the brush bounds; if not, reset the zoom.
  observeEvent(input$plot1_dblclick, {
    brush <- input$plot1_brush
    if (!is.null(brush)) {
      ranges$x <- c(brush$xmin, brush$xmax)
      ranges$y <- c(brush$ymin, brush$ymax)

    } else {
      ranges$x <- NULL
      ranges$y <- NULL
    }
  })

}

shinyApp(ui, server)

The biggest advantage we get out of Pro is the ability to use more server resources (with better managed resources too). We kept getting bottlenecks when more than one user was accessing the server. With Pro, our performance is limited primarily due to our data sources (and my programming ha ha).

messages.subject: Re: Shiny Sever Pro. vs. free version
messages.subject_clean: Shiny Sever Pro. vs. free version
messages.body_plain:
- Pro allows you to scale your applications to be able to support more than one user at a time (as Laz said), which is a really important feature if you plan on having your apps used by multiple people.
- It also lets you easily monitor your applications usage with a nice user friendly dashboard that shows you how your resources are being used and how many people are using which apps.
- Another very useful feature with Pro is that it gives you the ability to authenticate users - meaning you can place any shiny app you have behind a mandatory "log in" screen so that only people in your organization will be able to access the apps.
- And lastly, as Laz said, you will get priority support from RStudi and I can tell you first-hand that their support is absolutely fantastic and they'll go beyond your expectations in trying to help you if you have problems

I don't think you can easily have both versions running on the same machine, usually if you install Pro it will overwrite the free version

messages.subject: How to generate a random phone number using Shiny?
messages.subject_clean: How to generate a random phone number using Shiny?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am very new to Shiny and so far all I've learned to do is upload a CSV file.  But that's not why I'm here.

I'll be honest and say that when I am in the early phases of learning a new programming language or a package like R I get overwhelmed by the documentation so I get my feet wet by running examples and taking them apart.  Once I feel safe with that I don't get overwhelmed by the documentation.  <- this is a consequence of a mild dyslexia.  I know this is a very compartmentalized way to learn and doesn't even try to give a fundamental understanding of how it works.  I'll start getting the fundamentals by applying the pieces I learn to independent practice and eventually reading documentation.

So, I've learned to ask coding communities for help.  That's why I am here today.

I am hoping someone can provide me with a relatively simple example of generating a random phone number, where inputs are country code, area code, central office code, and the number of integers to randomize.  For example, country code for US is +1, the area code for Massachusetts is 351, the central office code for town of Rockport is 205, and then there are 4 numbers to randomize.

The result would be:

+1 - 351 - 205 - xxxx

I am imagining the app looks something like this:

Country Code:   +1

Area Code:  351

Central Office Code:   205

How many numbers to randomize?    4

[Run_Button]

Random Phone Number
[ +13512057493 ]

I know it's a big thing to ask if someone could code this for me, but I really do learn well this way.  This is how I learned R to begin with, which I use extensively now.  So, I would be grateful if I could learn from you.  I can tell you that once I take apart the pieces of the code I am asking for I will use pieces of them in other apps I try to write for practice.

Thanks for reading,

Jen

messages.subject: Shiny CRUD and Concurrency
messages.subject_clean: Shiny CRUD and Concurrency
messages.body_plain:
How does Shiny deal with concurrency issues? Let's say that I have a csv file that contains a list of names and ages. When I start my Shiny app, I load the csv into a data frame and allow users to insert, delete, or modify the data frame. When they're done, they hit a button and the relevant changes are made in the csv file. What happens if someone else opens the app at the same time and also makes some modifications? Is the data frame shared between the two instances of the Shiny app? Or are they completely independent? It seems like CRUD operations in a concurrent environment would something baked into the technology, but I haven't been able to find much on the topic beyond a blog post here: http://ipub.com/shiny-crud-app/

Regards,
Matt

messages.subject: Unexpected behavior of leaflet in a shiny app
messages.subject_clean: Unexpected behavior of leaflet in a shiny app
messages.body_plain:
Following the Leaflet for R/ Shiny Integration documentation <https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/shiny.html>, I'm getting unwanted/ unexpected behavior with the leafletProxy function.

In the app below, I'd expect the circle markers to appear/ disappear as the input$choices changes.

The reactive df 'filteredData' seems to be working correctly.

Am I incorrectly using leafletProxy() or clearShapes()?

library(shiny)
library(dplyr)
library(leaflet)

my_df <- data.frame(lat = 34.72 + rnorm(1000, sd = .18),
                    lng = -92.5 + rnorm(1000, sd = .33),
                    category = c(rep("A", 300), rep("B", 300), rep("C", 400)))

ui <- bootstrapPage(
  tags$style(type = "text/css", "html, body {width:100%;height:100%}"),
  leafletOutput("map", height = '100%', width = '100%'),
  absolutePanel(top = 10, right = 10,
                checkboxGroupInput("choices", "Choices", choices = list("A","B","C"), selected = c("A","B","C")),
                verbatimTextOutput("my_rows")

  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  filteredData <- reactive( my_df %>% filter(category %in% input$choices) )

    output$map <- renderLeaflet({ leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% setView(lat = 34.72, lng = -92.5, zoom = 9) })

    observe({

      leafletProxy("map", data = filteredData()) %>% clearShapes() %>% addCircleMarkers(radius = 6, weight = 1, fillColor = "red", fillOpacity = 0.3)

    })

    output$my_rows <- renderPrint({ filteredData() %>% nrow() })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

Hi Eva,

We run them both off of the same server, but our authentication methods are different for each one.  But if your goal is to have both authenticate using Active Directory, I would recommend setting up PAM authentication to use LDAP.  That method will vary based on what your linux distribution is.

I have not tested it, but with PAM using LDAP, you should be able to have users log in with their Active Directory credentials for either RStudio Server or Shiny Server.  (Someone please correct me if I am wrong.)

Hope that helps.

messages.subject: Re: Shiny Server and RStudio Server on the same system
messages.subject_clean: Shiny Server and RStudio Server on the same system
messages.body_plain:
Eva, I am no expert on AD or PAM, but you could technically use your own personal AD account strictly to bind to AD for authentication purposes. Or simply as proof of concept for AD authentication for Shiny and RStudio.

Depending on how your organization has its AD set up, you may have certain security requirements. But by default, you can bind with your user (for example, "cn=Eva User,cn=Users,dc=example,dc=corp" and your password), and use that to search your AD for user accounts and other things.

Most default AD environments do not allow any password changes or anything of that level of security without domain admin privileges. But strictly to search AD to find user accounts and for authentication, you should be good.

There are special cases that may require you to export/import your domain's SSL certificates, but as Joe has said, you should talk to your domain admin for that. If that's the case, you will just need to export the certificate for a domain controller (through mmc.exe) as a PEM format. And then copy that file to your Linux server and then install it on that Linux server so it trusts AD (if SSL/TLS is required by your admin). We have to do that for all of our AD domains.

We are very familiar with Ubuntu and Debian Linux environments, so I don't know if we can be of a lot of help to you on RedHat or CentOS (can't remember which you use) ...

If you have any simple questions (I'm a novice compared to most), feel free to reach out. I can possibly point you in the right direction at least.

~ Laz Peterson
Paravis, LLC

messages.subject: Re: Unexpected behavior of leaflet in a shiny app
messages.subject_clean: Unexpected behavior of leaflet in a shiny app
messages.body_plain:
This issue was solved on StackOverflow here <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/40207329/how-to-correctly-clearshapes-in-leaflet-in-a-shiny-app>.

I needed to 1) use clearMarkers() instead of clearShapes(), and 2) first check the reactive df wasn't empty with an if statement.

Complete corrected code is below:

library(shiny)
library(dplyr)
library(leaflet)

my_df <- data.frame(lat = 34.72 + rnorm(1000, sd = .18), lng = -92.5 + rnorm(1000, sd = .33), category = c(rep("A", 300), rep("B", 300), rep("C", 400)))

ui <- bootstrapPage(
  tags$style(type = "text/css", "html, body {width:100%;height:100%}"),
  leafletOutput("map", height = '100%', width = '100%'),
  absolutePanel(top = 10, right = 10,
    checkboxGroupInput("choices", "Choices" , choices = list("A","B","C") ,
      selected = c("A","B","C")),
    verbatimTextOutput("my_rows") )
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  filteredData <- reactive({ my_df %>% filter(category %in% input$choices) })

messages.subject: Re: Shiny CRUD and Concurrency
messages.subject_clean: Shiny CRUD and Concurrency
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

Some quick thoughts:
"Is the data frame shared between the two instances of the Shiny app? Or are they completely independent?" That depends of where your data lives. See this article about scoping in Shiny: http://shiny.rstudio.com/articles/scoping.html. Long story short, if you want your object accessible by all sessions, you should declare it outside the `ui` or `server` variables. Then, if you want the changes to be reflected across all sessions you need to use the super-assign operator <<- inside of the server function. Note that if you are reading from a csv and storing that in a variable like `mydata` (which is what is actually used in the app and can be modified with <<-), that will not change the underlying csv unless you do something like write.csv.
"It seems like CRUD operations in a concurrent environment would something baked into the technology." Hmmm, we don't really have anything else besides the default that the most recent operations wins (as the article you linked to states "the last person to click submit will simply win, and possibly overwrite another users changes without noticing"). You could implement your own custom behavior for dealing with concurrency, but I'd strongly recommend against this for things like files (you'd have to get into diff'ing algorithms for one thing). If that's important for you, checkout an actual database system and see how ti handles transactions and concurrency. Shiny works fairly well with RDBMSs, especially though DBI and dplyr. See this series of articles: http://shiny.rstudio.com/articles/#databases
Hope this helps!
Barbara

On Friday, October 21, 2016 at 2:19:42 PM UTC+1, Matthew Tardiff wrote:
> How does Shiny deal with concurrency issues? Let's say that I have a csv file that contains a list of names and ages. When I start my Shiny app, I load the csv into a data frame and allow users to insert, delete, or modify the data frame. When they're done, they hit a button and the relevant changes are made in the csv file. What happens if someone else opens the app at the same time and also makes some modifications? Is the data frame shared between the two instances of the Shiny app? Or are they completely independent? It seems like CRUD operations in a concurrent environment would something baked into the technology, but I haven't been able to find much on the topic beyond a blog post here: http://ipub.com/shiny-crud-app/
>
> Regards,
> Matt

messages.subject: Re: reactive() and render...()?
messages.subject_clean: reactive() and render...()?
messages.body_plain:
You can think of renderXXX({...}) as creating a reactive expression. That is probably the most useful way to think about things.

But as a matter of implementation, it's not actually true. It just so happens that outputs are implemented using observers, and renderXXX only needs to return a function, that will be called from within that observer. (Very early versions of Shiny actually called these reactiveXXX, as in output$plot <- reactivePlot(...).)

I can prove it:

> is.reactive(renderText("hi"))
[1] FALSE
> is.function(renderText("hi"))
[1] TRUE

So this actually works, though we don't recommend this syntax:

output$foo <- function() {
  input$x
}

This works too and is (I think) more readable, hence recommended, but isn't technically necessary:

output$foo <- reactive({
  input$x
})

In a way, outputs/renderXXX are really their own thing. They're similar to reactive expressions except that you can't use them in other reactive expressions or other outputs (i.e. they don't compose). And they're similar to observers except that you don't actually do side-effecty things inside of them.

Inside of Shiny there's a method called defineOutput, and output$x<-y is actually a call to defineOutput(x, y). It looks essentially like this (OK not really but this gives you the basic idea):

defineOutput <- function(name, renderFunc) {
  observe({
    value <- renderFunc()
    browser$updateOutput(name, value)
  })
}

So the renderXXX functions take a code chunk, and return a function that is used as the "renderFunc" in the code snippet above.

messages.subject: Re: Shiny and parallel processing
messages.subject_clean: Shiny and parallel processing
messages.body_plain:
Hey there Joe ~

We had a spreadsheet for end-of-year gifts for referring businesses.  This data was then put into a database, and we are now rendering “tiles” through Shiny for each referring business that show the amount of referrals and payments they have generated throughout 2015 and 2016.  These tiles also have a list of the gifts given at the end of 2015, and then buttons to select the gifts they wish to send at the end of 2016.

There are roughly 260 total referring business.  I’m getting closer by making lists of lists, storing them as reactive values (and then unlist()-ing them), so we’re at about 17 seconds now to create the full page.

But realistically, this processing should actually be done in less than 2 seconds on the very very very slow end.  withTags() and the related operations are wonderful, though they would be even better if there was something we can do for performance. :-)

My only issue is that I’m dealing with very impatient people, and when something pops up and it takes more than a couple seconds, they get really angry.  No worries — if there’s nothing we can do to speed up the tags, we’ll deal with it as it is.  But after this project, I’m actually thinking we will be using this method more and more, as it is AWESOME for putting together basic apps!

Thanks Joe!

~ Laz Peterson
Paravis, LLC

messages.subject: Re: reactive() and render...()?
messages.subject_clean: reactive() and render...()?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the very detailed answer Joe, I learned a lot from it

On Thursday, 27 October 2016 18:30:29 UTC-4, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> You can think of renderXXX({...}) as creating a reactive expression. That is probably the most useful way to think about things.
>
> But as a matter of implementation, it's not actually true. It just so happens that outputs are implemented using observers, and renderXXX only needs to return a function, that will be called from within that observer. (Very early versions of Shiny actually called these reactiveXXX, as in output$plot <- reactivePlot(...).)
>
> I can prove it:
>
> > is.reactive(renderText("hi"))
> [1] FALSE
> > is.function(renderText("hi"))
> [1] TRUE
>
> So this actually works, though we don't recommend this syntax:
>
> output$foo <- function() {
>   input$x
> }
>
> This works too and is (I think) more readable, hence recommended, but isn't technically necessary:
>
> output$foo <- reactive({
>   input$x
> })
>
> In a way, outputs/renderXXX are really their own thing. They're similar to reactive expressions except that you can't use them in other reactive expressions or other outputs (i.e. they don't compose). And they're similar to observers except that you don't actually do side-effecty things inside of them.
>
> Inside of Shiny there's a method called defineOutput, and output$x<-y is actually a call to defineOutput(x, y). It looks essentially like this (OK not really but this gives you the basic idea):
>
> defineOutput <- function(name, renderFunc) {
>   observe({
>     value <- renderFunc()
>     browser$updateOutput(name, value)
>   })
> }
>
> So the renderXXX functions take a code chunk, and return a function that is used as the "renderFunc" in the code snippet above.
>
> On Wed, Oct 26, 2016 at 5:44 PM 3D0G <tom.we...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Yesterday I watched Joe Cheng's videos from the 2016 Shiny developer conference (https://www.rstudio.com/resources/webinars/shiny-developer-conference/). I don't think I understood reactivity at all until I watched his two videos.
> >
> > Today I've been playing with what I learned. But I don't understand why he didn't say something like "all the render... commands also create reactive expressions." Maybe I missed it? Maybe I misunderstand render functions?
> >
> > Are there other commands that create reactive expressions besides reactive() and the render...() group?
> >

Hi Ken, RStudio Server is a different piece of software than Shiny Server. The former is used to interactively work with an R session as is you're running RStudio on your desktop; one of the features is that you (as an RStudio user) can run Shiny apps as if from your own desktop. The latter is used to make your Shiny app generally available to anyone with a web browser.

See:
https://www.rstudio.com/products/shiny/download-server/
http://docs.rstudio.com/shiny-server/#quick-start

messages.subject: Re: How to run long R Scripts with Shiny
messages.subject_clean: How to run long R Scripts with Shiny
messages.body_plain:
Hello Shelley —

Where does the user’s datasets come from?  Do they upload them through the Shiny interface, or is it something they have in a database or on a network share somewhere?

There are a lot of limitations on the user’s connection and session.  You probably don’t want to leave it up to chance if the user closes their browser window.

We have a few things that run processes that may take a bit of time (2 hours is probably the longest).  So on our Shiny server (note: we should probably have this actually running on a different server), we have a cron job that runs once every 5 minutes and checks for CSV files in a folder, which is a mounted network share.  If the cron script sees that a new file exists and is no longer open or accessed, it it moves the file elsewhere and then starts processing.  We also do this with data in MySQL databases.  If there’s something waiting to be dealt with, it goes into a queue and gets processed.

In your case, the Shiny side of it could take the user’s data and put it in a “holding tank” on a database server somewhere to await processing, in a format quite native to R, and also index that user’s request with the data (email address, requested job task, data, etc) to send the results to when it’s done, or do whatever other task would be next.  The cron script would run an R script that would check if there are any data waiting to be processed, figure out which data would be processed the quickest, then prioritize and start the processing (of course sending the results to each respective user when it’s done).

Just an idea.

~ Laz Peterson
Paravis, LLC

messages.subject: Re: How to run long R Scripts with Shiny
messages.subject_clean: How to run long R Scripts with Shiny
messages.body_plain:
Hey there Shelley --

Your users could have (for example) access to some network share or somewhere on the server that they could save their files. And your script could start (before the Rscript part) by doing a "find" command for any files sitting in that folder. That's just an idea ... but you could definitely have it run on a single cron job.

Either make sure their data gets stored as a file in a specific location on the server, or I would recommend setting up a MySQL server and then using DbWriteTable (or is it DbCopyTable?) functions to just throw it into the database server. Much easier accessed that way.

If your front end app could simply accept their data and place it as a file on the server or into a database, the cron script could run and just check those locations for anything that needs to be processed. You'll just need a way of defining which user is waiting for the results from which files - either putting this information as metadata inside the file name, or having a database table linked with that information. That's a discussion we could have another time. (If you're interested in the database method, I can explain how we do ours in private emails.)

The big issue you're facing is making sure that if they do not wait for processing to finish before closing their browser, the data could go into the oblivion. So to have a reliable system, it will definitely have to have a few moving parts. A Shiny front end is great, with a cron-style R back end.

We used to have our data stored as files, but the more you work with, the harder it is to deal with. Databases are great because we can index each dataset and flag it as new, processed, processed but not reported yet, etc.

Learning dplyr, DBI and pool package functions will get you sorted proper with the database input and output.

It's been a long week, so I'm probably not making any sense at this point ha ha. But feel free to ask any questions you like.

Have a great weekend.

~ Laz Peterson
Paravis, LLC

messages.subject: How to use the reactive output in an R script
messages.subject_clean: How to use the reactive output in an R script
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

I have created an shinyapp that supports the user to download trading data from a suppliers API.
The purpose is to make the user input user friendly and the shiny app together with R code builds up  the needed URL
(which is printed out at the bottom of the app).

I know that in the Shiny tutorial it is mentioned that the result of reactive expression can be re-used using data(). In my case I use data1.
Since shinyapp obviously prints out the result the usage of data1 is working.

Question: How can I use the result of the reactive expression in another R script.
I would like to avoid putting the complete script inside of shiny environment since my download script
will be used by other scripts and environments outside of shiny.

My code:

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  # 1st tab - Download Data - OHLC

  tabsetPanel(
    tabPanel("Download OHLC", tags$br(),
             h4("Fill in all the values and hit button-step1. "),
             h4("At the bottom of this page you find your generated url."),
             h4("The generated url will be used with an R script to trigger the download"),
             dateInput(inputId = "date.from.1", "Date(from):", "Date(from):"),
             dateInput(inputId = "date.to.1", "Date(to):", "Date(to):"),
             selectInput(inputId = "pr.1", "Product", c("[Select]"="[Select]", "Sweden" = "IX.D.OMX.IFM.IP")),
             selectInput(inputId = "tr.1", "Time resolution", c("[Select:]" = "[Select:]",
                                                                "30 minutes" = "MINUTE_30",
                                                                "15 minutes" = "MINUTE_15",
                                                                "5 minutes" = "MINUTE_5")),
             submitButton("Step1 - Build URL string"), # Button
             tags$br(), # line break
             tags$br(), # line break
             submitButton("Step2 - Download data (not active yet!"), # Button
             tags$br(), # line break
             textInput("", "Search for a product/article:", "")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      textOutput("text1")) # Repository
  ))

server <- function(input, output) {

  data1 <- reactive({
    paste0("\"https://demo.api.ig.com/gateway/deal/prices/",input$pr.1,"?","resolution=",input$tr.1,"&","from=",input$date.from.1,"&","to:",input$date.to.1,"\"")
  })
  output$text1 <- renderText({
    data1()
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
